proof:
**Volume and integer fibers.** The center $c_D=(11/36,1/18,\ldots,1/18)$ lies strictly inside $D$. Reflection in it exchanges both bounds on each coordinate, and changes the coordinate sum $s$ to $25/18-s$, exchanging the bounds $7/18$ and $1$. Thus $D$ is centrally symmetric. It lies inside $B$. For fixed $(x_2,\ldots,x_8)\in[0,1/9]^7$ and $s'=\sum_{i=2}^8x_i$, the interval for $x_1$ has endpoints $\max(0,7/18-s')$ and $\min(11/18,1-s')$. Its length is $11/18-|s'-7/18|$, which is at least $2/9$ throughout the cube. If $T$ is the sum of seven independent uniform variables on $[0,1]$, this gives
$$
|D|=9^{-7}\left(\frac{11}{18}-\frac19\mathbb E|T-7/2|\right),
\qquad
\mathbb E|T-7/2|=\frac2{8!}\sum_{j=0}^3(-1)^j\binom7j(7/2-j)^8
=\frac{113149}{184320}.
$$
For the expectation, symmetry reduces the integral to twice the mean of $(7/2-T)_+$. Adding an eighth integration variable realizes its integral over the positive orthant as simplex volume. Excluding the sets where any of the first seven coordinates exceeds one by inclusion-exclusion yields the displayed sum. Substitution gives $|D|=900611/7934371614720$ and $2^7|D|/(\Gamma V)=6304277/4194304>3/2$.

The stated $q$ equals $\Gamma V/(2^7\lambda^8|D|)$. Since $\lambda^8\ge 21/25$, this gives $0<q<1$. Hence $C$ is centrally symmetric, has volume $2\Gamma V$ and has center $c_C=(11\lambda q/18,\lambda/9,\ldots,\lambda/9)$. All its coordinates are nonnegative, their sum is at most $2\lambda$, and $x_i\le 2\lambda/9$ for $i=2,\ldots,8$. The midpoint sum $(A+C)/2$ is in $B$ because its coordinates are nonnegative and their sum is at most $\lambda+4\varepsilon=123/125<1$.

The base projection of the lifted hull is $[-1,1]$. At either endpoint, extremality of the base forces the given fiber. In a convex combination with base zero, the two endpoint coefficients are equal, so their contribution is a scaled point of $(A+C)/2$. Combining it with a point of $B$ stays in $B$. The three prescribed fibers are therefore exact. The hull is rational since each generator is a rational polytope. It is compact and full-dimensional because it contains a full-dimensional simplex in the middle plane and a point off that plane.

For a centrally symmetric full-dimensional body its center has half the volume in every through-center halfspace. At any point one of two opposite through-point caps has at most half the volume. This gives $A(A)=a/2$ and $A(C)=\Gamma V$. The simplex case of 03bc771bddd39a8a applies to the full-dimensional $B$ in dimension eight and gives $A(B)=\Gamma V$. The comparison threshold is $\tau=(A(A)+A(B)+A(C))/2=\Gamma V+a/4$.

**Nine caps over the middle base.** Write $\ell_0(x)=1-\sum_{i=1}^8x_i$ and $\ell_i(x)=x_i$ for $1\le i\le8$. Set $\alpha=a/V=40320/10^{24}$, $k=7/(81\Gamma)$, $j=2/(81\Gamma)$, $b_h=1/9+k\alpha$ and $b_l=1/9-j\alpha$. The exact comparisons $1/3<\Gamma<2/5$ and $0<\alpha<1/1000$ give $0<k,j<1/3$ and $0<b_l<b_h<1$. The thresholds satisfy $2b_h+7b_l=1$.

For $i=0,1$ use $H_i=\{(z,x):\ell_i(x)-2z\ge b_h\}$. On the small endpoint $A$, both linear tests are at least $2$ because $\ell_0\ge1-8\varepsilon>0$ and $x_1\ge0$. On $C$, the two tests are at most $1-2$ and $2\lambda-2$, respectively, both strictly below $b_h$. Thus each cap contains all of $A$, excludes all of $C$, and has mass $V(1-b_h)^8+a$. The middle trace formula follows because $\{\ell_i\ge b\}\cap B$ is the image of $B$ under the homothety of ratio $1-b$ about vertex $i$.

For $i=2,\ldots,8$ set $\beta=\varepsilon/2-\lambda/9$ and use $H_i=\{(z,x):x_i+\beta z\ge b_l\}$. At either endpoint the test is at most $\varepsilon/2+\lambda/9$. The positive gap is
$$
b_l-\left(\frac\varepsilon2+\frac\lambda9\right)
=\frac1{450}-\frac1{2000}-j\alpha
>\frac1{450}-\frac1{2000}-\frac1{3000}
=\frac1{720}.
$$
Hence each of these caps excludes both endpoints and has mass exactly $V(1-b_l)^8$. The nine closed caps cover all of $B$ because a point outside them at base zero would have a sum of barycentric coordinates strictly below $2b_h+7b_l=1$.

For $c=8/9$, the derivative of $t^8$ at $c$ is $8c^7=9\Gamma$ and its second derivative is at most $56$ on $[0,1]$. The two arguments $c-k\alpha$ and $c+j\alpha$ are in this interval. Taylor's bound and $k,j<1/3$ give
$$
(c-k\alpha)^8+\alpha\le\Gamma+\frac29\alpha+\frac{28}{9}\alpha^2,
\qquad
(c+j\alpha)^8\le\Gamma+\frac29\alpha+\frac{28}{9}\alpha^2.
$$
Indeed $9\Gamma k=7/9$ and $9\Gamma j=2/9$. Therefore the nine cap masses are bounded by $U=\Gamma V+(2/9)a+28a^2/(9V)$. The comparison is strict since $(\tau-U)/a=1/4-2/9-(28/9)\alpha>37/1500$.

**Four endpoint caps.** For each sign, the cap $\{\pm(x_1-\varepsilon/2)-2(z+1)\ge0\}$ cuts half of $A$. These two caps together cover $A$. On $B$ their affine tests are bounded above by $1-2<0$ since $x_1\in[0,1]$. On $C$ both tests are at most $2-4<0$ since $x_1\in[0,2\lambda]$ and $\lambda<1$. Each cap has mixed mass $a/2$.

Write $c_1=11\lambda q/18\in(0,1)$. For each sign, the cap $\{\pm(x_1-c_1)+2(z-1)\ge0\}$ cuts half of $C$ by central symmetry. These two caps together cover $C$. On $B$ and $A$, respectively, their tests are bounded above by $1-2<0$ and $1-4<0$ because $x_1,c_1\in[0,1]$ there. Each cap has mixed mass $\Gamma V$. Both endpoint cap budgets are at most $U$ since $\alpha/2<\Gamma$.

The thirteen fixed closed halfspaces cover all feasible points, so $h_S(y)\le U$ for every $y\in S$. A maximum exists because $S$ is compact and depth is upper semicontinuous. In fact one may move every containing halfspace parallel to itself through $y$. For each fixed nonzero normal, the mass of the resulting closed cap is upper semicontinuous in $y$ by the pointwise upper limit inequality for closed cap indicators and finiteness of $\mathcal H_8(S)$. The infimum over these normals is upper semicontinuous as well.

Every ambient closed halfspace containing $(1,c_C)$ contains either the entire fiber at base $1$ or a continuous halfspace through or beyond its center on the containing side. Thus it captures at least $\Gamma V$, and either of the two endpoint caps at base $1$ realizes equality. Since $\mathcal H_8(S)=(1+2\Gamma)V+a$ and $\alpha<1-2\Gamma$, this depth strictly exceeds $(\Gamma/2)\mathcal H_8(S)$.

statement:
Let $A(K)$ denote the maximum ordinary raw halfspace depth of a full-dimensional convex body $K$. In $\mathbb R^8$ let $B=\{x:x_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^8x_i\le1\}$, $V=1/8!$, $\Gamma=(8/9)^8$, $\varepsilon=1/1000$, $A=[0,\varepsilon]^8$, and $a=\varepsilon^8$. Define
$$
D=\left\{x: 0\le x_1\le\frac{11}{18},\
0\le x_i\le\frac19\ (2\le i\le8),\
\frac7{18}\le\sum_{i=1}^8x_i\le1\right\},\qquad
C=2\lambda\operatorname{diag}(q,1,\ldots,1)D,
$$
where $\lambda=49/50$ and $q=163840000000000000000/209509599832532483477$. The convex hull of the lifts of $A,B,C$ at $-1,0,1$ is a rational convex body in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^8$ with exactly those three integer fibers. Let $S$ be their union with these lifts, and $h_S$ its raw depth under $\mathcal H_8$.
$$
\Gamma V
\le \max_{y\in S}h_S(y)
\le \Gamma V+\frac29 a+\frac{28a^2}{9V}
<\frac{A(A)+A(B)+A(C)}{2}-\frac{37}{1500}a .
$$
The depth at the center of the exposed fiber $C$ is $\Gamma V$, which exceeds $(\Gamma/2)\mathcal H_8(S)$.
title: Actual mixed depth below half the sum of own maximal depths
